name: Long fire and reflector
summary: A fire as long as you are, with a wall behind it and a shelter behind you — the difference between a fire you sit at and a night you sleep through.
time: 1-2 hours to build, then feeding through the night

materials.item: green logs or stones for the reflector

steps.text: Understand the problem first: a campfire radiates. You get hot on one side and lose heat off the other into the dark, and to the GROUND, which takes more than the air does.
Build the fire LONG — a trench or line of fire roughly your own body length, not a cone. A point source warms a point; a line warms a line.
Raise a REFLECTOR wall on the far side: green logs stacked between two pairs of driven stakes, or rocks, or an earth bank. Lean it slightly toward the fire.
steps.why: Radiant heat that would have gone into the night comes back across the fire to you. It roughly doubles what reaches your side and it shelters the fire from wind.

steps.text: Sleep on the near side, with your shelter or a second reflector behind YOU so heat is trapped between two surfaces.
Put a thick bed of boughs or litter under you — a hand-span compressed. This matters MORE than the fire.
steps.why: Conduction into cold ground outpaces radiant gain from the flames. People with a good fire and no bedding still get hypothermic, all night, every year.

steps.text: Set the fire an arm's length away — close enough to feel it on your face, far enough that a spark does not land on you.
Feed it with big pieces laid ALONG the line rather than across, so it burns down the length rather than out into a heap.

verify: Lie down where you intend to sleep and check the heat reaches your feet as well as your chest. If it does not, the fire is not long enough.
Put a hand between your bedding and the ground after twenty minutes. If the ground is cold there, you need more under you, not more fire.
The reflector should be warm to the touch on its fire side after half an hour.
limits: A long fire eats fuel — plan on gathering several times what a cooking fire needs, and gather it BEFORE dark.
It is a heat source, not a shelter. In wind or rain it needs both a reflector and something over you.
Nobody sleeps straight through beside a fire. Expect to wake and feed it; that is the design, not a failure.
cautions: Rocks from a riverbed or any waterlogged stone can EXPLODE when heated — trapped water turns to steam. Use dry rock from high ground, and never put your face over a fresh rock ring.
A reflector of green logs will eventually dry and catch. Check it.
Sparks and a synthetic sleeping bag are a bad pairing; a hole burns through in an instant and the fill melts.
Do not build a long fire over roots or deep duff — it can travel underground and surface hours later.
